# Describing data I {.hero #s01-visualisation}

::: {.sem-mark data-sem="1"}
Seminar 1 · Data visualisation
:::

A histogram is a choice, not a fact.

::: {.lede}
The worksheet asks which display suits which data. The harder question is what happens *after* you pick one — because the same thirty numbers can be made to tell two different stories.
:::

## The same 30 numbers, three ways {.stage-slide #bins-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="bins-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bins-frag-w1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="bins-frag-w2"}

::: {.slide-footer}
Nothing was added or removed between the second and third views. Only the bin width changed — and with it, whether you would report a long right tail at all.
:::

## Turn the knob yourself {.sim-slide #bins-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 1 · binning
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-plot}
```{webr-r}
#| fig-width: 5.7
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: "100%"
set.seed(7)
x <- round(rgamma(120, 2.2, 0.45) + 4, 1)
bw <- 1   # <-- bin width
brk <- seq(floor(min(x)),
           ceiling(max(x)) + bw, bw)
hist(x, breaks = brk, col = "#CBD9E6",
     border = "white", las = 1,
     main = paste("bin width =", bw),
     xlab = "R&D spend (% of revenue)")
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
Run it with `bw <- 1`, then `0.5`, then `5`. At which width does the right tail stop being visible? That is the width an optimist would choose.
:::
